newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia dlr recovers slowly on Japan demand.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia dlr recovers slowly on Japan demand.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished Friday on a relatively robust note having recovered almost all the ground lost during the rout of US$/yen last week.

It finally recaptured the 79 cent barrier courtesy of persistent samurai-related demand, which saw around A$1.0 billion worth of bonds launched this week and convinced at least one big U.S. seller to withdraw for the moment.

More samurai issues were believed to be in the pipeline for next week, but dealers cautioned the local currency would be hard pressed to sustain further gains above US$0.7920 chart resistance while US$/yen remained so fragile.
By 5.30 pm (0630 GMT) the local dollar had struggled to US$0.7904/09 from Thursday's late US$0.7897/02 and US$0.7832/37 this time last week.

Support was expected at US$0.7890 with US$0.7860 seen as the key trip-wire level for bears, while the next major resistance level was US$0.7920 which bulls needed to breach to signal a fresh uptrend to US$0.7985.

On the crosses it was stuck at 88.06/16 yen from Thursday's 88.19/29, having never stirred far from last Friday's 87.90/00 through the week as the U.S. dollar remained under pressure despite a chorus of supportive comments from G3 officials.
The U.S. dollar was cushioned by a torrent of supportive comments from Japanese, German and U.S. officials, including Treasury Secretary Rubin who said he favoured a strong dollar.
But much of the good work was undone by speculation economist Fred Bergsten was in line for a high profile place in President Clinton's administration.
Bergsten has been an outspoken proponent of a weaker dollar as a means of correcting Japan's huge trade surplus.
Back at home, the flow of secondary economic data continued with September manufacturing input prices, import prices and private sector credit figures all out.
The secondary figures on inflation and lending suggested to analysts that scope existed for a further cut in official interest rates.
Manufacturing input prices fell 0.5 percent in September and dropped 4.1 percent in annual terms, while import prices slid 0.7 percent for a whopping 6.4 percent fall on the year.
The data reinforced the subdued inflation message delivered by manufacturing output prices earlier in the week which were up only 0.5 percent on the year.
In both cases the strength of the dollar had been the key restraining influence on prices.
And, with the currency defying all attempts to drag it lower, the stage looked set for favourable inflation outcomes for the next couple of quarters at least, said analysts.
Data on private sector credit also showed a slowing in the pace of lending growth in September to an annual 11.4 percent from 12.8 percent the month before.

Consumer and business lending both rose a relatively modest 0.5 percent, while credit for housing was up only 0.4 percent suggesting the long awaited recovery in the housing market would be a slow one.
